section_summary: Pages 79–105 continue and conclude an April 1946 registry of Japanese publishers, giving their addresses, representatives, and publication specialties in Tokyo and numerous prefectures. Page 106 is a December 1947 State Department despatch transmitting a SCAP survey of Japanese news agencies. The enclosed survey traces the development of Japanese news services from the pre-Domei era through Domei’s wartime monopoly and dissolution, the creation and operation of Kyodo and Jiji, and the proliferation of smaller specialized agencies after the war.

subfiles.title: Registry of Japanese Publishers, Addresses, and Representatives (continued)
subfiles.about: Continuation of an alphabetical and prefecture-by-prefecture registry of Japanese publishers, their addresses, representatives, and publication specialties.
subfiles.summary: The directory completes its Tokyo entries from publishers beginning with T through Z and then lists publishers outside Tokyo by prefecture or city. Each entry normally supplies a publisher’s name, street address, representative, and a letter code for publication specialty. The provincial portion ranges from Aichi and Aomori through Yamaguchi and includes newspaper companies, universities, scholarly societies, manufacturers, religious bodies, and individual publishers.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1463: Survey of Japanese News Agencies
subfiles.from: Acting United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Transmits five copies of a SCAP Civil Information and Education Section survey of Japanese news agencies.
subfiles.summary: Despatch 1463 sends a November 28, 1947 SCAP Civil Information and Education survey of Japanese news agencies, outlining their development and important agencies and listing those operating on March 1, 1947.

subfiles.title: A Survey of Japanese News Agencies
subfiles.from: Information Media Research, Analysis and Research Division, Civil Information and Education Section, General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: Historical and organizational survey of Japanese news agencies from their nineteenth-century origins through the early Allied Occupation.
subfiles.summary: The report traces Japanese news agencies from Teikoku, Dentsu, Kokusai, Toho, and Rengo through the government-backed formation of Domei, describing Domei’s nationwide and overseas infrastructure, wartime monopoly, propaganda role, censorship, and October 1945 dissolution. It then explains the division of Domei’s assets and personnel between Kyodo and Jiji, detailing their ownership, governance, staffing, finances, communications networks, foreign-news sources, services, and noncompetition agreement. Organization charts and traffic maps document Kyodo’s and Jiji’s national operations. The closing pages discuss the influence of numerous smaller specialized agencies and begin a profile of Radiopress, the former Foreign Office shortwave-monitoring service.
